planting.note: Move dormant tubers or potted divisions into saturated, perpetually cool seep soil right after the ground softens, before the summer dry-down begins.

directions: This terrestrial orchid grows in the perpetually saturated seeps and fen edges of the Klamath-Siskiyou region, including serpentine-fed bogs where Darlingtonia also grows, and sends up a dense spike of fragrant white-to-cream flowers in early summer. Give it year-round seepage or a bog-pot setup rather than ordinary garden soil, since the roots never tolerate drying out. It tolerates filtered woodland light better than open glare and resents being disturbed once established. Mulch lightly with sphagnum or coarse sand to keep the crown from rotting while still holding moisture.

planting.note: Set rooted stolons directly into mucky, continuously moist fen or seep margins; this species spreads on its own once the soil stays wet.

directions: A low creeping violet of boggy meadows and shaded seep margins across the Klamath-Siskiyou and much of the cool temperate northern hemisphere, it produces small pale lilac flowers with darker veining just above its heart-shaped leaves. It spreads by slender surface stolons into a loose mat and does best where the soil never fully dries, even in dappled shade at a bog garden's edge. Use it as a living mulch at the drip line of taller fen perennials where its shallow roots won't compete for the same moisture layer. Divide congested clumps in early spring to keep it from smothering smaller neighbors.

planting.note: Start plugs under cover and transplant after frost into open, mineral-rich wet meadow soil that stays saturated through late spring.

directions: Bolander's Horkelia forms a low mat of strawberry-like foliage topped with small cream flowers in the open, sunny wet meadows and serpentine seeps of the northern California Coast Ranges and Klamath-Siskiyou. It wants full sun and standing winter moisture but can handle the gradual summer drying typical of seasonal seep sites once roots are established. Because it tolerates the magnesium-heavy, nutrient-poor chemistry of serpentine-derived soils, it holds its own against grasses that would otherwise crowd a richer wet meadow planting. Leave the foliage rosettes undivided for a few seasons to let the mat fill in before any thinning.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in autumn into a seasonally wet meadow pocket that floods in winter and drains dry by midsummer, mimicking its native cycle.

directions: This small onion grows scattered through vernally saturated meadows and serpentine seeps of the Klamath-Siskiyou and adjacent North Coast Ranges, pushing up grassy leaves and a tight pink-to-rose umbel just as the ground begins to dry out. It needs winter and spring wet feet followed by a genuinely dry summer dormancy, so pair it with other geophytes rather than plants that need steady moisture year-round. Western native-bulb specialists occasionally list it for rock garden and seasonal wetland plantings where its bloom adds color right as spring ephemerals fade. Mark the dormant spot so summer cultivation doesn't disturb the resting bulbs.

planting.note: Sow directly into cold, saturated fen or seep soil in fall so seed overwinters naturally; germination follows the following spring thaw.

directions: This Klamath-Siskiyou fringed grass-of-parnassus sends up wiry stalks of white flowers with distinctive hair-fringed lower petals from a basal rosette, flowering in late summer in the wet meadows, fens, and serpentine seeps scattered through the Klamath-Siskiyou and Cascade ranges. It needs consistently cold, saturated, mineral-rich soil and struggles anywhere the ground warms or dries in summer, making it a good companion for sedges and sundews at a bog garden's margin. Light overhead shade from nearby shrubs mimics the partial cover of its native seep sites without shading out the bloom. Established clumps self-sow modestly along the same saturated zone rather than spreading aggressively.

planting.note: Move divisions into a shaded, year-round wet seep or fen pocket as soon as the soil is workable; this saxifrage will not establish in soil that dries between waterings.

directions: Bog Saxifrage holds a flat rosette of broad leaves close to the mud and sends up a tall, airy stalk of small white flowers well above the foliage, a familiar sight in the montane bogs, seeps, and serpentine fens of the Klamath-Siskiyou and Cascades. The rosette itself wants constant saturation and benefits from the light shade cast by taller fen companions, which keeps the crown from scorching during the brief summer warm spell. It reads best massed at the saturated edge of a bog garden where the flower stalks can rise above lower groundcovers like marsh violet. Keep the crown free of heavy leaf litter over winter to prevent rot.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions into permanently saturated, acidic-to-serpentine sphagnum fen soil, the same conditions it shares with Darlingtonia in the wild.

directions: California Bog Asphodel is a rhizomatous fen specialist that forms grass-like tufts topped with short spikes of starry yellow flowers, growing alongside the California pitcher plant in open, sun-drenched serpentine and sphagnum fens of the Klamath-Siskiyou. It spreads slowly by rhizome through permanently waterlogged, mineral-poor substrate and does not tolerate any summer drying, so it belongs in a true bog planting rather than an ordinary moist border. Carnivorous-plant and bog-garden specialty growers that stock Darlingtonia companions sometimes carry it for exactly this pairing. Keep standing water or a perpetually wet sphagnum mat around the rhizomes through the growing season.

planting.note: Sow or set divisions along a saturated seep or streambank with serpentine-influenced soil chemistry; it spreads by stolons once the site stays reliably wet.

directions: Oregon Willowherb is a narrow fireweed relative restricted to serpentine seeps, fens, and streambanks of the Klamath-Siskiyou in Del Norte, Curry, and Josephine counties, where it spreads by stolons and opens magenta-pink flowers through summer. It is listed as rare by the California Native Plant Society, so stock typically comes from a handful of regional native-plant specialty growers rather than mainstream retailers, and plants should only be sourced as nursery propagated material, never wild-collected. It needs the same permanent seepage and partial overhead cover from surrounding shrubs or conifers that it gets in its native fens. Because its range is so narrow, treat it as a conservation-minded specimen rather than a mass planting.
